summary.text: The characteristic polynomial of a square matrix is a polynomial that has the matrix's eigenvalues as its roots.
It has the determinant and the trace of the matrix among its coefficients, and it stays the same when the matrix is replaced by a similar one.
Setting it equal to zero gives the characteristic equation, and for a linear map on a finite-dimensional space it does not depend on the choice of basis.

items.prompt: Two matrices are similar to each other. What can you say about their characteristic polynomials?

options.label: They are exactly the same polynomial
They share only the same degree
They differ by a constant factor
They share nothing in general

items.explain: Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial; it does not change under similarity.

items.prompt: Two matrices turn out to have exactly the same characteristic polynomial. Must they be similar?

options.label: Yes, the polynomial identifies a matrix up to similarity
Yes, but only when the matrices are square
No, but they must then be equal
No, equal polynomials need not mean similar

items.explain: Similar matrices share a polynomial, but the converse is not true in general.

items.prompt: You factor a matrix's characteristic polynomial and find its roots are 2 and 5. What have you found?

options.label: The trace and the determinant
Two eigenvectors of the matrix
The eigenvalues of the matrix
A basis for the vector space

items.explain: The eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial.

items.prompt: You have the characteristic polynomial and want the equation whose solutions are the eigenvalues. What do you do?

options.label: Square it and then divide by its degree
Set the polynomial equal to zero
Add up all of its coefficients
Differentiate it once and solve

items.explain: Equating the characteristic polynomial to zero gives the characteristic equation.

items.prompt: Two students write the same linear map on a finite-dimensional space as matrices, using different bases. Will their characteristic polynomials differ?

options.label: Yes, each basis gives its own polynomial
Yes, but only in the constant term
No, but only if the bases are orthogonal
No, the polynomial does not depend on the basis

items.explain: The characteristic polynomial of a linear map is the same over any basis.

items.prompt: Astronomers once used the characteristic polynomial under another name to calculate slow changes in planetary orbits over centuries. What was that name?

options.label: Secular function
Orbital equation
Spectral polynomial
Determinantal root

items.explain: It was called the secular function because it served to compute secular perturbations of planetary orbits.
